name: Sediment Sound Group
description:
Sediment Sound Group is one of Vantablack Media's most visible Circuit-facing subsidiaries, operating out of a mid-rise tower in the upper Circuit district with a roster that skews toward working-class comfort music, blues-adjacent neural folk, and the kind of earnest, politically inoffensive Shelf-adjacent sound that corporate lawyers have pre-approved for mass distribution. Founded in 2201 as part of Vantablack's 'authentic roots' initiative — a PR campaign designed to counter accusations that the conglomerate was strangling independent music — SSG was built to look independent without being independent. Its branding is deliberately worn-in, its logo hand-drawn in style, its offices decorated with retro vinyl and handwritten lyrics framed behind glass.

In practice, SSG operates a sophisticated content review pipeline that filters out political language, anti-corporate sentiment, and any material that references specific Tier 1 infrastructure failures or corporate negligence. Artists signed to Sediment often describe a slow erosion of their material — songs arrive with notes, notes become suggestions, suggestions become contractual requirements. Several prominent Circuit artists have walked off the roster citing creative interference, most notably Okafor & The Driftline, who released a scathing open mesh-letter in 2218 before signing with the pirate-adjacent Lowline Press. Despite this reputation, SSG's distribution reach is enormous, and for artists from the Circuit who want legal neural feed placement, Sediment remains one of the only viable paths.
creator: Vantablack Media
genre: Neural folk, Circuit blues, working-class comfort, acoustic drone
audience: Tier 2 and Tier 3 workers, Circuit residents seeking emotionally resonant music without political edge, older listeners who remember pre-corporate indie scenes
cultural_impact: Sediment Sound Group represents the most visible example of corporate co-optation of Circuit culture in GLMZ. Its existence has sparked ongoing debate about authenticity, access, and the cost of distribution reach — whether an artist who signs with SSG is selling out or simply surviving. Among the Circuit's working musicians, 'going Sediment' has become slang for compromising your material in exchange for stability, carrying both judgment and a kind of exhausted sympathy.
known_fans: Corporate HR staff who curate office ambient feeds
Tier 3 commuters on the rail lines
Older Circuit residents who distrust pirate feeds
Municipal workers who want legal background music for long shifts
story_hooks: A beloved Circuit artist has just signed with SSG and their longtime fans are divided — some see betrayal, others see survival. A journalist embedded in the scene must decide whether to publish a leaked copy of the artist's contract, which contains disturbing content restriction clauses.

An SSG A&R scout is quietly approaching underground artists in Tier 1 with offers that seem too generous — players in the scene suspect Vantablack is trying to buy out and shelf promising voices before they become politically dangerous.

A data archivist at SSG discovers that the label has been quietly burying master recordings of artists who left the roster — not destroying them, but locking them in a licensing limbo that prevents re-release. She has the access codes to free them.
